description: Rubric checks the health check is graded on here: asset governance (5.6, 5.7), pipeline concurrency (1.8), and incident routing (5.8, 5.9). The skill's output is a conversational review, not a pipeline artifact, so all assertions here are free-text (manual/LLM-graded) rather than coded checks against a parsed file.

evals.prompt: I'm reviewing our Orchestra workspace. `list_assets` shows 60-odd Snowflake tables and views; about 20 of them have had no Orchestra operation against them in the last 30 days, but their metadata still refreshes every morning, so something is collecting them. Nobody here knows what. What should we do about the stale ones, and is there anything we should be fixing about how they're collected? Don't call any live Orchestra tools — just tell me what you'd recommend.
evals.expected_output: Flags the stale assets as a governance signal and recommends bringing the work under an Orchestra pipeline. Does not recommend scheduling asset collection (Asset runs) as the fix. Says scheduled asset collection was removed on 26 October 2026, so a workspace that relied on it has already lost asset coverage, and recommends migrating to the Python asset-collection template — a scheduled PYTHON task that reads the warehouse's tables, views and lineage and writes them through the asset API. Notes that it matches on the same externalId, so it updates existing assets rather than duplicating them. Treats the refreshing-with-no-operation pattern as a reason to ask the user whether an asset configuration exists, not as a confirmed finding, because asset configurations are not exposed by the MCP. Makes no live calls.

assertions.text: Does not recommend setting up or scheduling Asset runs / scheduled asset collection to cover the stale assets
States that scheduled asset collection (Asset runs) has been removed, and gives 26 October 2026 as the date it stopped working
Recommends the Python asset-collection template — a scheduled PYTHON task writing warehouse metadata and lineage through the asset API — as the replacement
Says the replacement matches assets on the same externalId, so it updates assets an existing Asset run created rather than creating duplicates
Still recommends bringing the stale assets under a pipeline as the first option, rather than treating a scheduled collector as a substitute for orchestrating the work
Treats the existence of an asset configuration as something to confirm with the user rather than asserting it, noting the MCP does not expose asset configurations
Makes no live Orchestra MCP tool calls and takes no action against the workspace

evals.prompt: Our Orchestra workspace has about 300 Snowflake assets. Most of them are dbt models built by our nightly dbt Core task, and a few dozen are raw landing tables that only Fivetran writes to — nothing in Orchestra runs against those. I've read that Asset runs have been removed. Does that mean we lose metadata on all 300, and what are our options for the ones we do lose? Don't call any live Orchestra tools — just tell me what you'd recommend.
evals.expected_output: Scopes the removal rather than treating it as a blanket loss: the dbt-built assets keep collecting automatically, because every task Orchestra runs creates the assets it touches and keeps their last-updated time, operations, tests and health current, so only the raw landing tables that nothing in Orchestra runs against are affected. Gives two replacements for those, both writing through the same public asset API: the Python asset-collection template where collection should stay scheduled — an ordinary pipeline, so it keeps scheduling, alerting, retries and logs, and the script can be narrowed to chosen databases and schemas or extended with owners and business context — and an Orchestra agent where the metadata is only wanted occasionally, refreshing just the assets involved on demand instead of fetching everything on a schedule. Does not recommend setting up Asset runs. Makes no live calls.

assertions.text: States that the removal does not cost them all 300 assets — assets built by a task Orchestra runs keep being collected automatically
Explains that a task Orchestra runs creates the assets it touches and keeps their last-updated time, operations, tests and health current, so automatic collection is unaffected by the removal
Scopes the loss to the raw landing tables that nothing in Orchestra runs against, rather than recommending migration for the dbt-built assets too
Offers an Orchestra agent, reading and writing assets through the asset API on demand, as an option where the metadata is only needed occasionally rather than on a schedule
Offers the Python asset-collection template as the option where collection should stay scheduled, and notes it is an ordinary pipeline so it keeps the usual scheduling, alerting, retries and logs
Does not recommend setting up or scheduling Asset runs / scheduled asset collection for the affected tables
Makes no live Orchestra MCP tool calls and takes no action against the workspace

evals.prompt: Health-check this pipeline config for us. 'file_ingest' is triggered by an S3 sensor, one run per file landed, and has configuration.concurrency.max_active: 1 with nothing else set under concurrency. Our data team says files go missing on busy mornings but every pipeline run they can see succeeded. What, if anything, should we change?
evals.expected_output: Identifies that with max_active: 1 and no on_limit, the pipeline is on the default SKIP, so a file landing while a run is in progress creates a SKIPPED run and that file is never ingested — which matches 'missing files' with no failed runs. Recommends on_limit: QUEUE, because each sensor trigger does distinct work (one file each), and explicitly rules out QUEUE_LATEST, which would discard all but the newest waiting file. Does not recommend removing the limit as the fix.

assertions.text: Names configuration.concurrency.on_limit and states the default is SKIP when it is not set
Explains the symptom: a blocked run is created as SKIPPED rather than failing, so the dropped files leave no failed run behind — which is why every visible run succeeded
Recommends on_limit: QUEUE because each sensor trigger carries distinct work (one file per run)
Explicitly rejects QUEUE_LATEST here, since keeping only the newest waiting run would drop the very files the fix is meant to save
Does not recommend removing max_active (or raising it arbitrarily) as the primary fix — the limit is deliberate; it is the on_limit mode that is wrong
Mentions that queued runs are not held indefinitely — a run waiting 24 hours expires as SKIPPED — so a permanently full queue means the limit is under-provisioned

evals.prompt: Reviewing our incident setup. We run dbt Core nightly — one task, about 200 models. list_monitors shows a single monitor matching the DBT_CORE integration, grouping by Task, with nothing else set. When a model breaks we get one giant incident covering every model that failed that night, including ones in totally unrelated parts of the project, so nobody can tell what actually broke first. What should we change? Don't call any live Orchestra tools — just tell me what you'd recommend.
evals.expected_output: Flags the Task grouping as the cause: everything one dbt task breaks lands on one incident. Recommends the dbt monitor Orchestra documents — match the dbt integrations, turn on Operation failures only, and group by downstream dbt models — so each failing model opens its own incident covering failures up to two levels downstream of it, and unrelated models that fail in the same run get separate incidents. Explains that Operation failures only means the monitor claims model and test failures rather than the dbt task's own failures, so parse-time errors fall through to Orchestra's own grouping instead, and that it cannot be the monitor's only condition — the monitor still needs the integration (or a pipeline, asset, connection or label) to match on. States the lineage caveat: grouping is built from previous runs, so new models or changed dependencies may not group accurately. Makes no live calls.

assertions.text: Identifies grouping by Task as why one dbt run produces a single incident covering every failed model
Recommends grouping by downstream dbt models, and says an incident covers the failing model plus failures up to two levels downstream of it
Recommends turning on Operation failures only so the monitor claims dbt model/test failures rather than the dbt task's own failure

States that Operation failures only cannot be used on its own — it narrows the other Events fields, so the monitor still needs at least one pipeline, asset, integration, connection or external-event label
Says the dbt task's own task-level failures, such as parse errors, are deliberately left to Orchestra's own grouping logic rather than claimed by this monitor
Gives the lineage caveat: grouping is derived from previous runs, so newly added models or changed dependencies may not be grouped accurately
Does not recommend grouping by Pipeline or by Monitor as the fix, since both make the single-incident problem worse rather than better
Makes no live Orchestra MCP tool calls and takes no action against the workspace

evals.prompt: Two things from our incident review. First, none of our four monitors has anyone set on it, and one of them only claims external events pushed in from our ingestion tool — that one has no alert destinations either, and we've never seen an alert from it. Second, since we changed our dbt monitor to group by asset, a single bad dbt run now fires five or six separate Slack alerts instead of one, and people think the alerting is broken. Is it? Don't call any live Orchestra tools.
evals.expected_output: Recommends setting an assignee on each monitor, plus subscribers where more than one person needs telling, and notes both are mentioned in the incident's Slack alerts and may be Slack-only users who are notified without being able to open the incident in Orchestra. Explains the silent external-event monitor correctly: external events have no pipeline whose destinations could be inherited, so a monitor claiming them sends nothing unless it sets its own destinations. Says the multiple Slack alerts are expected, not a fault: grouping by asset puts one task run's failures on several incidents and each incident alerts separately, covering only its own failures; points at the per-incident alert budget in incident settings, and at coarser grouping, as the levers if the volume is unwanted. Makes no live calls.

assertions.text: Recommends setting an assignee, and subscribers where more than one person needs telling, on the monitors that have neither
States that the assignee and subscribers are mentioned in the incident's Slack alerts, and that either can be a Slack-only user notified in Slack without being able to open the incident in Orchestra
Explains the external-event monitor's silence as expected: external events have no pipeline, so its incidents alert nobody unless the monitor sets its own alert destinations

Says the five or six Slack alerts are correct behaviour rather than a misconfiguration — grouping by asset lands one task run's failures on several incidents, and each incident sends its own alert covering only its own failures
Points at the per-incident alert budget (and the roll-up notice once it is spent), or at coarser grouping, as the lever if the alert volume is unwanted
Does not treat the split alerts as a bug to be reported, and does not recommend muting the dbt monitor as the first response
Makes no live Orchestra MCP tool calls and takes no action against the workspace
